To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the promotive effect on germination of high temperature before or after germination induction in celery seeds is due to the prevention of the imposition of dormancy at high temperature and the prevention of damage due to drying.

(1) high temperature prevents germination even if given after germination induction, but germination occurs if the seeds are then returned to 16°C; (2) seeds incubated for three days at 16°C and then air dried at 20°C for three days germinate slowly when re-sow at 16°C in white light; (3) exposure of such seeds to high temperature (32°C), prior to and during air drying, results in 50% seed germination
the promotive effect on celery seed germination of treating them with 32°C is due to the prevention of the development of dormancy, which is induced by 17°C and light.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the promotive effect of high temperature on subsequent germination was due to a combination of two mechanisms, namely: (a) a conditioning of the seed coat to withstand desiccating damage, and (b) the removal of dormancy.
the promotive effect of heat treatment of celery seeds is a result of a combination of factors.

a high temperature treatment (32°C for 3 d) of celery seeds before or during drying is beneficial to germination and that the treatment is effective even if applied after 4 d germination induction at low temperature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the promotive effect of high temperatures on subsequent germination is not restricted to the period of imbibition but may occur at any time before and during drying.
the promotive effect of a germination-induction treatment on subsequent germination can be maintained even after the seeds are dried and stored for 1 yr.

the promotive effect of high temperature is due to its ability to prevent the imposition of dormancy and to overcome the effects of desiccation damage, but not to its effect in breaking dormancy per se.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high temperature (32°C for 2–4 d) is an effective method for breaking dormancy of celery seeds, even if the seeds are dried at high temperature.

the promotive effect on the subsequent germination of celery is due to a conditioning effect of high temperature on the seeds, and that the promotive action of high temperature is independent of the induction of dormancy at 35°C.
the use of heat treatments to break dormancy in celery seeds can result in a significant improvement in germination performance.
